title: Know Your Simile
paragraphs: > Four are the grounds for comparison > Between the tenor and the vehicle: > The deed done, the effect thereof > The form and the complexion.
A simile compares something with something else using the words like or as, for example,
a row of teeth like a string of pearls
Here ‘a row of teeth’ is the subject of comparison, and ‘a string of pearls’ is the simile or the standard of comparison.
In Sanskrit, the subject of comparison is called uvamēyam and the standard of comparison is known as upamānam. These terms are frequently used in the teaching of similes.

Comparisons are made between things on the basis of four common characteristics, viz., complexion, form, deed and effect. The comparison markers in Tamil are aṉṉa, āṅka, pōla, etc. (meaning like or as)
e.g. mayilaṉṉa cāyal - peacock’s like grace māṉ pōlat tuḷḷiṉāl - she hopped like a deer.
Tolkāppiyar in the verse quoted above speaks of the classification of similes.

This classification comprises (i) comparison of things that are accessible to the eyes, and (ii) comparison of things that are accessible to other sense organs or to the mind. We shall illustrate these classes and the grounds for comparison.

She flew off as a sparrow (comparison based on deed) • munificent like rain (comparison based on effect) • neck like a conch (comparison based on form) • gold-like complexion (comparison based on colour)

flute’s like speech (through hearing) • sweet like honey (through taste) • scorching like the summer sun (through bodily feeling) • fragrant breeze (through smell) • O lovely moon! Is the joy of your sight Like the joy of sighting A potful of white rice While looking for A little gruel in hunger? (through the mind)
Apart from these that we have drawn on the first verse of Tolkāppiyam : Uvamaiyiyal, the second verse speaks of the mixed categories of similitude:
> The grounds for comparison above > Do get intermingled too.
